Our static-site release has two steps, and the order matters.

**1. Upload all new assets under versioned names.** Each new JS, CSS, image or other file gets a name that includes its version (for example `app.3f9c2.js`). That way it never overwrites a file a live page might be using. Nothing points to these files yet, so uploading them has no effect on users.

**2. Switch the manifest to the new names.** The manifest is what pages read to find out which asset files to load. Once it changes, browsers that fetch it start requesting the new files.

**Why the upload comes before the switch:** if the manifest changed first, browsers would ask for files that don't exist yet and get 404s, which means broken styles, scripts or images. Uploading first ensures every name the new manifest refers to is already there, so the switch takes effect all at once with no broken window.

**Why we keep the old assets:** some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch, from an open tab or a cached copy. They will keep requesting the old versioned files until they reload. If we deleted those files, those users would get 404s partway through a session. Leaving the old assets in place lets those pages keep working while users gradually pick up the new manifest.

Each release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first because the manifest is what browsers follow. Once it points at the new names, any browser that loads it will immediately request those files. If any of them aren't uploaded yet, those requests fail and the page breaks. Uploading first means everything the new manifest references already exists the moment it goes live. That makes the switch a single atomic change from a complete old release to a complete new one.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running the site. A user who loaded the page before the switch still holds the previous manifest. Their browser will keep requesting the old names, for example when it lazy-loads a script or fetches an image on navigation. If we deleted those files, those users would get 404s partway through their session. Because each release uses new versioned names, keeping the old files never conflicts with the new release. Our releases happen in two steps, in this order:

**i1 Upload first.** Every new asset goes up under a versioned name (for example, `app.3f9c.js`) before anything points to it. The manifest is what tells browsers which files to load. If we switched it first, browsers would request files that don't exist yet and the page would break. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when the manifest goes live.

**i2 Then switch the manifest.** This single change is the release. Because the new files are already in place, the switch is effectively atomic: a browser gets either the old manifest or the new one, and every file each one names is available.

**i3 Keep the old assets.** A browser that loaded the previous manifest before the switch will keep requesting the files that manifest names, such as lazy-loaded chunks, images, and stylesheets. If we deleted those files, users partway through a session would get 404s. Since versioned names never collide, old and new files can sit side by side, and both manifests keep working.

A release has two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name, then switch the manifest to point at those names.

The upload comes first so that every name the new manifest references already exists the moment the manifest goes live. If the manifest switched first, a browser could load it and request a file that isn't uploaded yet, and get a 404 or a broken page. Because new assets go under new versioned names, uploading them changes nothing for current visitors. They're invisible until the manifest points at them, so the switch is the single moment the release takes effect.

We keep the old assets because the switch doesn't reach browsers that already have the previous manifest. A page loaded a minute before the release still references the old names and may request more of them later, such as a lazy-loaded script, a stylesheet, or a code-split chunk on navigation. If those files were gone, that session would break mid-use. Leaving them in place lets older sessions keep working until they reload and pick up the new manifest. It also makes rollback simple, since we can point the manifest back at the previous names without re-uploading anything.
